name: Kumara Bhimeswara Swamy Temple, Samalkota
deity: Shiva worshipped as Kumara Bhimeswara, with his consort Bala Tripura Sundari
period: Eastern Chalukya, late 9th–early 10th century CE (Chalukya Bhima, r. c. 892–922)
dynasty: Eastern Chalukya (later Kakatiya and Nayaka renovations)
summary: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, Kumararama at Samalkota raises a towering monolithic linga through two storeys — installed, tradition says, by Kartikeya himself, the warrior god from whom the temple takes its name.

sections.history: The Kumara Bhimeswara Swamy temple was raised by the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in the late ninth and early tenth century, its founding traditionally linked to the reign of Chalukya Bhima (c. 892–922 CE), whose name it also carries as Bhimarama. It is one of the five Pancharama Kshetras, the ancient Shiva sanctuaries scattered across coastal Andhra, and among the group it is distinguished by the scale and ambition of its central shrine. Successive dynasties tended it across the centuries: its pillars carry inscriptions dated between 1147 and 1494, recording gifts under the Kakatiyas, the Reddi kings and the Nayaka rulers who followed. Standing at Samalkota — the old Samarlakota — the temple has remained in continuous worship for more than a thousand years, and today the Archaeological Survey of India protects it as a centrally protected monument of national importance: a rare living shrine that is also a first-rank monument.
sections.architecture: The temple's defining wonder is its sanctum, built in two storeys around a single towering linga. Carved from a monolith of pale limestone and rising some fourteen to sixteen feet, the linga passes up through the ceiling of the ground floor, so that daily worship is offered on the upper storey where its crown emerges — the signature 'linga through two floors' that sets Kumararama apart within the Pancharama circuit. Before the shrine spreads a great mandapam borne on a hundred carved pillars, several bearing inscriptions across the centuries, and at the entrance kneels a monolithic Ekasila Nandi, cut from a single stone. The whole is worked in the Dravidian idiom the Eastern Chalukyas favoured — a blend of Chalukyan and Chola sensibilities — with later Kakatiya and Nayaka hands adding to the fabric. Restrained yet monumental, it is built around a single vertical axis of devotion.
sections.legends: Kumararama belongs to the great origin story shared by all five Pancharama shrines. The asura Tarakasura wore a Shiva linga that made him invincible, and in battle Kartikeya — Kumara Swamy, the warrior son of Shiva — could not slay him until Vishnu revealed that the linga must first be broken. Kartikeya shattered it with his fiery weapon, and it split into five pieces that fell across the Andhra coast; over each a temple rose. Here at Samalkota, tradition holds that Kartikeya himself installed the linga he had struck down, and from Kumara Swamy the shrine takes its name Kumararama — binding the town's temple to a warrior god and to its four sister sanctuaries along the coast.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple's great night, when devotees keep vigil and abhishekam flows over the towering linga through the dark hours. Each year around February and March a Kalyana Mahotsavam celebrates the divine marriage of Kumara Bhimeswara and Bala Tripura Sundari with processions and ritual splendour, and special abhishekams are offered in the months around November and December. Through the year the two-storey sanctum draws pilgrims making the Pancharama round.
sections.experience: To visit Kumararama is, quite literally, to climb toward the divine. Enter past the single-stone Nandi, cross the hundred-pillared hall, then ascend to the upper storey to stand level with the crown of the great linga — a rare sensation of meeting the deity at height rather than gazing down into a sunken sanctum. The consort Bala Tripura Sundari is honoured alongside. The temple sits in the busy town of Samalkota, easily reached and unhurried on ordinary mornings, and pairs naturally with the other four Pancharama shrines for pilgrims completing the circuit. Come early, when lamplight and the first abhishekam fill the twin storeys.

visit.timings: Open daily, roughly 6 am to 12 noon and again 4 pm to 8 pm; timings extend and mornings grow crowded on Maha Shivaratri and during the annual Kalyana Mahotsavam.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected; footwear is left outside before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas and courtyards, but not inside the inner sanctum where worship is offered.
visit.gettingThere: Samalkot Junction, a major railway junction, lies in the town itself, giving excellent rail access; the nearest airport is Rajahmundry (RJA), with Visakhapatnam (VTZ) about 130 km away, and the temple is an easy road trip within coastal Andhra.
